changelog: Replace E1 with measured example en_us_888 to teach moving cuts left onto non-assertive prefixes (addresses finding that scorer cuts after content heads).

Replace E2 with measured example en_us_741 to show danger of splitting numeric/measure phrases and the need to treat suffixes that can overturn factual claims as unsafe (addresses underweighted contra risk).
Replace E3 with measured example en_us_105 to illustrate high-contradiction suffixes (relative clauses like 'from which ...' that can negate or change preceding assertion).

Replace E4 with measured example en_us_924 to emphasize that suffixes supplying essential instrumentation or scope (e.g. 'that can be called ... without charge') raise contra and should be ranked unsafe.

findings: The scorer habitually prefers cutting after content heads instead of moving the cut left to leave a non-assertive / functional prefix; that choice produces fragments that assert misleading facts when the later piece arrives.
The scorer underweights high contradiction risk: positions whose suffix alone plausibly overturns or negates the prefix are being ranked safe despite high contra, which kills sets.

diagnosis.why: The new examples pushed the scorer to prefer earlier cuts on short pieces (≤3–7 words), which caused it to split predicates/negations away from their suffixes (e.g. isolating “diagnosis” from “cannot be made”) and so lowered H_set there, while the same changes encouraged merging adjacent content words and preserving enumerations in longer chunks (helping ≥10-word bins). This mixed effect produced a small net negative mean with harms concentrated in the shortest bins.
diagnosis.lesson: A later revision should avoid teaching a blanket leftward cut bias that isolates predicates/negations on very short pieces even if it helps merge noun compounds or enumerations in longer contexts.
